title: Multilevel versus single-level regression for the analysis of multilevel information: The case of quantitative intersectional analysis
abstract: Intersectional MAIHDA involves applying multilevel models in order to estimate intercategorical inequalities. The approach has been validated thus far using both simulations and empirical applications, and has numerous methodological and theoretical advantages over single-level approaches, including parsimony and reliability for analyzing high-dimensional interactions. In this issue of SSM, Lizotte, Mahendran, Churchill and Bauer (hereafter "LMCB") assert that there has been insufficient clarity on the interpretation of fixed effects regression coefficients in intersectional MAIHDA, and that stratum-level residuals in intersectional MAIHDA are not interpretable as interaction effects. We disagree with their second assertion; however, the authors are right to call for greater clarity. For this purpose, in this response we have three main objectives. (1) In their commentary, LMCB incorrectly describe model predictions based on MAIHDA fixed effects as estimates of "grand means" (or the mean of means), when they are actually "precision-weighted grand means." We clarify the differences between average predicted values obtained by different models, and argue that predictions obtained by MAIHDA are more suitable to serve as reference points for residual/interaction effects. This further enables us to clarify the interpretation of residual/interaction effects in MAIHDA and conventional models. Using simple simulations, we demonstrate conditions under which the precision-weighted grand mean resembles a grand mean, and when it resembles a population mean (or the mean of all individual observations) obtained using single-level regression, explaining the results obtained by LMCB and informing future research. (2) We construct a modification to MAIHDA that constrains the fixed effects so that the resulting model predictions provide estimates of population means, which we use to demonstrate the robustness of results reported by Evans et al. (2018). We find that stratum-specific residuals obtained using the two approaches are highly correlated (Pearson corr = 0.98, p < 0.0001) and no substantive conclusions would have been affected if the preference had been for estimating population means. However, we advise researchers to use the original, unconstrained MAIHDA. (3) Finally, we outline the extent to which single-level and MAIHDA approaches address the fundamental goals of quantitative intersectional analyses and conclude that intersectional MAIHDA remains a promising new approach for the examination of inequalities.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2019 article has achieved clear scholarly uptake, with 93 OpenAlex citations and standing in the top 10% of works for its field and year. Its influence is concentrated in methods- and equity-oriented health research, and it has also generated documented downstream reuse in preprints, reviews, and related articles. The record shows a focused methodological impact rather than broad public-facing attention.

Full narrative

Clare R. Evans, George Leckie, and Juan Merlo’s article on multilevel versus single-level regression for quantitative intersectional analysis has become a visible reference point for methodological work on intersectional inequalities. The strongest signal is scholarly uptake: the article has 93 citations in OpenAlex and is assessed as top 10% cited for its field and publication year, indicating sustained use by researchers working with multilevel and intersectional data.

The citation landscape suggests that the paper has been taken up most actively in health and equity research. It appears frequently in Social Science & Medicine and related venues, and the cited work topics cluster around health disparities and outcomes, LGBTQ health, racial and ethnic identity research, and sex and gender in healthcare. That pattern is consistent with the article’s core contribution: clarifying when multilevel modeling offers advantages over single-level regression for high-dimensional intersectional questions.

Evidence of reuse is also substantial. The work has been documented as reused in 100 downstream items, dominated by journal articles, with additional preprints and reviews. Recent citing papers show continuing methodological discussion as well as applied intersectional studies in healthcare, adolescence, and environmental justice, suggesting that the paper is being used both to justify analytic choices and to frame substantive research questions.

Public-facing attention is comparatively limited in the record available here. Scite reports mostly mentioning citations, with only a small number of supporting citations, and the event-data and broader public-discourse feeds do not provide additional signal. Taken together, the evidence points to a paper whose impact is primarily methodological and academic: influential within intersectionality, epidemiology, and quantitative social science, with especially strong resonance in health equity research.

The article’s open-access status is recorded as green, which likely supported reach, and it was funded by Vetenskapsrådet. Overall, the record shows a well-cited methods paper that has helped shape how intersectional inequalities are analyzed, especially where researchers need parsimonious and reliable approaches to complex interaction structures.
